title: Batching fairness memory surge — on-call diary and runbook draft
content:
Summary:

This is a working on-call diary and preliminary runbook draft for an incident class we've started seeing intermittently: a memory surge on a subset of serving hosts correlated with a degradation in batching fairness (long-lived tiny batches + a few huge batches), leading to increased p99 latency and occasional OOMs in multi-tenant hosts. Document captures observed signals, short-term mitigations used during last incident, triage commands, hypotheses, and proposed permanent fixes.

Why this doc exists:
- Previously handled incidents focused on KV cache evictions and prefetch races; this one has subtle interaction between continuous batching, routing fairness, and per-request memory amplification (KV cache + temp token buffers).
- We want an on-call checklist that is quick to follow when alerts trigger "mem-surge-batching" and a clear set of next actions for SRE/serving-engineering.

Incident overview (2024-11-14 02:12 UTC):
- Alert: host-group-prod-3 average memory used > 78% and sustained p99 latency for generate API > 650ms for 12m.
- Impact: ~12% of requests from region-us-west experienced increased latency; two worker containers crashed with OOM, Pod restarts with short availability blips (<90s). No customer-visible errors beyond latency for most routes.
- Immediate status: mitigated by routing traffic away from affected hosts and flipping a per-cluster batching-weight flag (see mitigations).

Observed signals and metrics: (what we looked at)
- host-level: top memory processes (python worker) grew from 4.2GB -> 14.1GB over ~9 minutes.
- per-worker heap: transient temp buffers allocated during batching coalescing (observed via tracemalloc sampling traces).
- batching distribution: metric batch_size_histogram skewed — many tiny batches (1-4) plus occasional very large batches (>128) that held onto large KV windows.
- KV cache hitrate: small degradation (~2%) but eviction rate spiked (evictions/sec x5).
- queueing: request queue depth increased, and fairness metric (per-tenant served ratio) showed a small subset of tenants getting bulked batching capacity.
- telemetry: number of active streams (streaming endpoints) stable — not the dominant factor.

Key timeline (UTC):
- 02:12: alert fires (memory > 78% and p99 > 650ms).
- 02:13: on-call (Ava) acknowledges, posts to #sre-oncall.
- 02:16: triage: confirm host cluster; check pod restarts, check trace samples.
- 02:20: flip routing weight to reduce traffic to host-group-prod-3 (fast mitigation).
- 02:24: enable temporary flag disable-batching-window-grow on cluster.
- 02:28: OOM kills observed on 2 pods; pods restart; rolling back some long-lived cache entries flagged earlier (see KV eviction toggles).
- 02:35: system stabilizes; memory usage trends down to 55% over 10 minutes; p99 returns to baseline.

Initial triage steps used (commands we ran):
- kubectl -n prod get pods -o wide --field-selector=status.phase=Running | grep host-group-prod-3
- kubectl -n prod exec -it <pod> -- sh -c "ps aux --sort=-rss | head -n 20"
- kubectl -n prod exec -it <pod> -- sh -c "pmap $(pgrep -f serving_worker) | tail -n 20"
- curl -sS http://metrics-host/metrics | grep batch_size_histogram -A4
- curl -sS http://tracing-host/samples?service=serving_worker | jq '.samples | .[] | {allocs:.alloc_count,trace:.trace_hash}' | head
- kubectl -n prod rollout restart deploy/serving-worker (only after routing and flags set as temporary mitigations)

Hypotheses (ordered):
1) Priority inversion in continuous batching: a small number of tenants produced many small requests that prevented the batching window from stabilizing, causing the batching algorithm to repeatedly coalesce and allocate temporary buffers that are not promptly released. Large occasional batches then needed big KV cache slices that amplified memory usage.
2) KV cache locking interplay: while batches are being assembled, workers hold transient references to large KVCache entries (prefetch windows) longer than expected; when eviction occurs concurrently it causes copying and memory amplification.
3) Compounded by microbatch path allocation regression introduced in PR #2431 — changes in buffer pooling reduced reuse under certain batch size distributions. (See linked PR).

Short-term mitigations (what we did in the incident):
- Reduce routing weight to affected cluster (automated route shift).
- Flip feature flag: batching-window-grow -> false (prevents runaway window growth).
- Reduce max batch size to 64 for a 10-min window via experiment control plane.
- Force local KV cache to prefer LRU with cap of 2000 entries for the cluster (temporary soft cap to reduce eviction churn).
- For pods with very high RSS, restart single pod to reclaim memory after routing reduction (prefer rolling restart).

Short on-call runbook (draft, follow this first):
1) Acknowledge the alert, post incident stub to #sre-oncall and ping serving-runtime on-call.
2) Identify affected hosts: kubectl filter by node label cluster=host-group-prod-3; collect pod names.
3) Immediately reduce routed proportion to the cluster: run routing CLI set-weight --cluster host-group-prod-3 --weight 20%. If automation is present, use autoswitch to safe pool.
4) Check batch_size_histogram metric: if p95 batch size < 8 AND p99 memory growth rate > 5%/min, flip flag batching-window-grow off: featurectl set batching-window-grow=false --scope cluster:host-group-prod-3.
5) If KV eviction rate spiked > 200/sec, apply temporary KV cap: kvctl set max_entries --cluster host-group-prod-3 --value 2000
6) If any worker RSS > 12GB and trending up, trigger rolling restart with 2s grace: kubectl rollout restart deploy/serving-worker --timeout=300s --max-unavailable=1
7) Monitor for 15 minutes; if memory continues to climb after routing weight change and flags, escalate to eng-serving-runtime, create P1 ticket, and consider draining nodes.

Diagnostics to collect (artifacts for postmortem):
- heap snapshots (tracemalloc) or core dump if reproducible.
- batch size histogram (1m/5m/15m windows).
- KV cache metrics: entries, evictions/sec, avg_entry_size.
- sampled traces covering the time window for allocations (attach trace hashes to Linear ticket).
- list of feature flags and rollout states at incident time.

Longer-term remediation candidates (proposal):
- Implement per-tenant batching credit system to enforce fairness (if tenant uses many small requests, cap coalescing rate).
- Add pre-allocated buffer pools for microbatch path to avoid repeated ephemeral allocs under high churn.
- Harden KV cache to avoid copy-on-evict under concurrent read+evict; prefer lock-free refcounts or atomic swap with staged reclamation.
- Improve telemetry: expose "batching fairness" metric (served_units_by_tenant / expected_share) and alert on skew.
- Add chaos tests for mixed batch distributions to CI e2e serving tests (simulate many tiny requests + occasional large requests to validate memory safety).

Open follow-ups and owners (triage board):
- S1: Short-term flag and autoswitch tuning: owner: Diego Martinez. Due: 2024-12-01.
- S2: Buffer pooling and microbatch allocation regression (PR 2431 follow-up): owner: Priya Kapoor. Due: 2025-01-15.
- S3: KV cache eviction rework (design doc): owner: Liam O'Neill. Due: 2025-02-10.
- S4: Post-incident runbook update and add playbook into SLO runbooks: owner: Ava Chen. Due: 2024-12-05.

Notes to on-call (tips learned):
- Don’t restart pods blindly if routing switch hasn't reduced load — restarts will come back under same pressure and may OOM again. Always combine restart with routing weight change or feature flag toggle.
- Flipping batching-window-grow off reduces throughput but stabilizes memory faster than capping KV entries. Use it as the first feature flag to try.
- Prefer rolling restart (one-at-a-time) to avoid mass restart causing flash-thrashing on autoscaler.

Sample Slack stub to post when incident is triaged:
"Incident: mem-surge-batching on host-group-prod-3. Routing weight reduced to 20%. batching-window-grow flag disabled for cluster. Restarting pods with RSS > 12GB one-by-one. Eng-serving-runtime pinged. Will update within 15m. Linked: RED-1892."

Appendix: quick reference commands
- routing CLI: rctl set-weight --cluster <name> --weight <percent>
- flag CLI: featurectl set <flag>=<value> --scope cluster:<name>
- KV cap: kvctl set max_entries --cluster <name> --value <n>
- collect traces: curl -sS "http://tracing-host/samples?service=serving_worker&since=15m" > /tmp/traces.json
- heap snapshot (if binary linked): python -m tracemalloc dump > /tmp/tracemalloc-$(date +%s).snap

Status: DRAFT. This doc should be reviewed with eng-serving-runtime and product (batching owners) before promoting to final runbook.

Revision history:
- 2024-11-15 Ava: initial draft, incident diary and mitigations captured.
- 2024-11-22 Priya: added hypothesis about PR-2431 regression and buffer pooling notes.
- 2025-01-08 Liam: added KV eviction caps and follow-up owners.

End of file.
